Locked Up for Good

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We go inside what's been described as the world's most humane prison and ask what lessons for a South African system apparently focused on retribution over rehabilitation.

Unique Selling Point:
Halden prison has opened its reinforced steel doors to Carte Blanche for a first-hand glimpse of Norway's approach to long-term incarceration. It's a maximum security facility but, in comparison to our own over-crowded, gang-ridden jails, it has the feel of a holiday camp. Prisoners are offered vocational training, yoga, lots of exercise and counseling services. Halden's governor insists that his staff are called "prison officials" rather than guards; an insight into an approach as far removed from the South African system as you're likely to get. An insight, too, into why Norway's re-offending rate among released inmates is just 20%. In South Africa, that rate is closer to 70%. We'll discover the secret to their success from the people who matter: the governor, the officials, and the prisoners.

Summary:
Norway is hardly a crime hot-spot. Its economy is strong and it has in place a generous social welfare system. So, comparisons with South Africa should be drawn with caution. But, like many societies (even the most flourishing) there are those who turn their backs on the benefits of being a law-abiding citizen and turn to a life of crime instead. And, for years, Norway believed the best way to deal with them was to exact retribution. Trouble is, the consequence of that approach - as it has been in America, South Africa and a myriad other countries - was to release back into society former inmates as unreformed and unrepentant as they had been when first sentenced. And that was measured in the numbers of those released from jail who went on to commit further crimes.

But a change in approach, one that emphasised rehabilitation and the notion that separation from society was punishment enough, achieved remarkable results. Norway now enjoys one of the lowest re-offending rates in the world and its prisons are regarded as among the world's most humane - with Halden the shining light.

What's more, the maximum sentence in Norway - for even the most heinous of crimes - is just 21 years (although, with a caveat that allows for maximum sentences to be subject to 5 year increments in the event of a prisoner not being rehabilitated).

Script:


Script for Carp – Halden
On screen text: “Recidivism – noun the tendency of a convicted criminal to re-offend.”
VO: Recidivism – it’s a fancy word that basically means the rate at which criminals who are released from prison go on to commit further crimes.
VO: The figure in South Africa is, well, alarming – according to some experts, as high as 85 to 95% among murderers, rapists and car-hijackers. Basically, our prison system – with some exceptions - is taking in violent people and merely spewing them out again. Change is clearly needed.
VO: You don’t have to spend too much time in Norway to realise it can teach us a thing or two about building a prosperous, functioning society.
VO: Perhaps unexpectedly, it’s got a few lessons about recidivism, too.
VO: While you should be cautious about making hard and fast comparisons between with South Africa and one of the wealthiest countries on the planet, when it comes to prisons and reducing reoffending rates, Norway is something of a world leader.
VO: So, I’m travelling south to find out how it got there.
(Pause)
VO: Hard as it is to imagine, Norway faced its own re-offending challenges. In the early 1980’s, its recidivism rate was around 60 to 70%. Their system, like ours, was broken.
Link I guess the temptation in a situation like that would be to clamp down even harder, impose stricter sentences, to withhold parole. But Norway did the precisely the opposite - and with considerable success – and the answer as to how lies just down this road.
VO: I’ve travelled about a hundred km’s south of Oslo to speak to some Norwegians who know a thing or two about helping to turn a recidivism crisis on its head.
Upsound Camera Op [Camera mic top of Carsten Jamissen interview C0024] “So camera is rolling…”
Upsound John Webb [Carsten Jamissen audio 200305_0021S1] 00:01 – 00:06 “Ok, audio all good? Happy with the camera, we’re rolling? We’ve got speed, great.
VO: In 2013, Carsten Jamissen raped, tortured and tried to kill a woman while visiting Brazil. He’s unsure why he did it, saying he may have been possessed. A year later, he was sentenced to two decades in prison.
VO: By the time judgement was handed down he’d been behind bars for over a year awaiting trial; already a veteran of Brazil’s notorious prison system and the brutality of some of its inmates.
ITV Carsten Jamissen [00:08:12] – Strap “Carsten Jamissen” one guy pushed me and when I turned around to him, the other guy came with a big stone to my head. You don't see it because of my hair, but my cranium is... *gestures* (CUT to reverse or wide) [00:11:21] people in prison areas have less value than a sh*t on the streets, you know, so they leave us to ourselves. So we have to, you know, make our own rules.
VO: Things could have gone from bad to worse for Carsten but, in 2018, the Norwegian government arranged his transfer here. A facility unlike any you’re likely to have seen.
Link – Think about every prison movie you’ve ever seen. Picture the razor wire, the watch towers, the snipers and guard dogs. Now empty your head of all those images because this is something completely different.
VO: This is Halden, often called the most humane prison in the world. It has the atmosphere of a university campus – an award-winning design purposely simulating life on the outside. Modern buildings surrounded by parkland- it’s, well, not much like a prison at all.
There are workshops, fully kitted and decorated visiting rooms, a larger guest house for overnight family stays and an impressive prayer room. Apparently, the architects tried to separate internal buildings to encourage inmates to walk – to strengthen their bond with the outside world. Oh, and it had a R16 million art budget in 2010. Some of it spent on these motivational murals.
VO: Carsten is one of 260 inmates.
Updound John “So this is your cell…”
VO: He arrived here 40kg lighter. Mentally weak, he says. Afraid to venture outside.
Uspound John “Is that you…”
VO: A picture on his wall shows a very different man staring through the bars of his Brazilian prison.
Upsound John “you were a lot thinner then? Carsten “yeah, even my father was concerned”
VO: The cells in Halden have flat screen televisions, dvd players, and en-suite bathrooms.
Upsound – John “that’s a well-stocked fridge”
VO: Oh, and they have fridges, too…
VO: …stocked with groceries bought at the prison store, paid for with money they’re given for attending work or educational activities.
VO: And as if that weren’t enough to convince you that Halden does confinement a little differently, the inmates are given the keys to their cells.
Usound – Carsten “ for example if I have to go somewhere to school or wherever, I lock it and put it in my pocket and go.”
VO: The guards, explains Carsten, retain a master key which allows them to keep the cells locked when required – which is generally 12 hours a day. Still, it’s an unusual practice considering this is a maximum-security prison housing some of the country’s worst offenders – from murderers to rapists.
VO: Every ten cells share a common room which wouldn’t look out of place in a middle-class apartment. There’s another flat screen tv, a seating area and a fully equipped kitchen.
VO: Linda Hansen is a correctional officer – the term guard is frowned upon here. Many of the officers at Halden are women, something their research shows discourages violence.
Upsound – [C0021 – 00:34] Linda “In all these activities we as correctional officers, we interact with them. So we play games, we watch tv, we sit and eat dinner with them. It’s like a family.
Upsound -John “Like a family, exactly. Well, you say that, but it is quite unusual to have a prison-type environment in a prison isn’t it
Upsound – Linda “Well yeah, but you can see it as children in a way. We just show them how normal life is.”
VO: The maximum sentence in Norway is 21 years – no matter your crime - so these prisoners will one day be someone’s neighbor. In other words, there’s method in this apparent madness.
ITV Are HØidal [00:19:15] I think that's very important that everyone have a future, everyone have possibilities to be released. If you know you shall sit in prison for life and never come out, you, of course, give up. And it's not important anything. What do you do? So I think that you have a hope, it's very important.
VO: Are Hoidal is Halden’s governor. The boss.
ITV Are HØidal [00:04:15] This prison is a high security prison. So it's a very important to take care of the security still, of course. But a very important part of the officer role is to work with change, change the inmate’s behavior... Change, motivate them to stop being criminals. To make a better future.
VO: It’s a television convention to introduce an interviewee by showing them working behind a desk but you get the impression it’s the last place Hoidal wants to be.
VO: Here he is with the American filmmaker, Michael Moore. Turns out I’m one of many who’s come knocking. A prisons veteran – familiar with the tough old days – he’s the face of a system that favours rehabilitation over punishment. And he doesn’t believe anyone is beyond redemption.
John Question (off camera) [00:14:55] Do you think that some prisoners are beyond rehabilitation?
Are HØidal [00:15:10] STRAP “Governor, Halden Prison” No, we think that everyone can change. We have programs for also sex offenders. Today we have programs running for sex offenders and then they give us feedback on that program and they say that program do something with them. So we believe that it's possible to also change sex offenders and pedophiles. We believe in that. So we have programs for that.
VO: Those programmes are run by professionals, but therapy of a more informal kind is left to officers like Linda.
ITV Linda Hansen [00:02:25] Strap “Linda Hansen, Correctional Official” Yeah, I've had a lot of good conversations with inmates and I think it's because they know us and they get to know us well so they know that they can trust us and then we will have a good conversation. So, yeah, I've had many of those. It's nice.
ITV Carsten Jamissen [00:33:00] – You know, at least here people have the chance to change, you know? And okay, everybody here knows they have done a crime, but should we get judged for that all the rest of our lives? Or should we get to start to get a second chance? [00:37:03] I've been in for two years now, I think I only see one or two guys a second time come back. In Brazil I see the same guy going back all the time.

VO: And that’s the clincher. This policy has reduced the recidivism rate in Norway to just 20%. And who would argue that a remorseful Carsten released in Norway will likely make a better neighbor than a hateful Carsten released in Brazil.
VO: But results like that come at a price. Norway spends close to R2 million/prisoner/year at Halden. The figure in South Africa is closer to R140 000. And one wonders whether a South Africa traumatized by crime is ready to cast aside a desire for retribution.
Link - I’m still trying to digest what I’ve seen today, and I’m assuming many of you at home watching consider it a system is a little too liberal. But the point is: for Norway it’s worked.
VO: At its centre is a change in attitude: treating people with respect and getting respect back. So perhaps, with some tinkering, it could work in South Africa too.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Halden prison has opened its reinforced steel doors to Carte Blanche for a first-hand glimpse of Norway's approach to long-term incarceration. It's a maximum security facility but, in comparison to our own over-crowded, gang-ridden jails, it has the feel of a holiday camp. Prisoners are offered vocational training, yoga, lots of exercise and counseling services. Halden's governor insists that his staff are called "prison officials" rather than guards; an insight into an approach as far removed from the South African system as you're likely to get. An insight, too, into why Norway's re-offending rate among released inmates is just 20%. In South Africa, that rate is closer to 70%. We'll discover the secret to their success from the people who matter: the governor, the officials, and the prisoners.
metadata.Summary: Norway is hardly a crime hot-spot. Its economy is strong and it has in place a generous social welfare system. So, comparisons with South Africa should be drawn with caution. But, like many societies (even the most flourishing) there are those who turn their backs on the benefits of being a law-abiding citizen and turn to a life of crime instead. And, for years, Norway believed the best way to deal with them was to exact retribution. Trouble is, the consequence of that approach - as it has been in America, South Africa and a myriad other countries - was to release back into society former inmates as unreformed and unrepentant as they had been when first sentenced. And that was measured in the numbers of those released from jail who went on to commit further crimes. But a change in approach, one that emphasised rehabilitation and the notion that separation from society was punishment enough, achieved remarkable results. Norway now enjoys one of the lowest re-offending rates in the world and its prisons are regarded as among the world's most humane - with Halden the shining light. What's more, the maximum sentence in Norway - for even the most heinous of crimes - is just 21 years (although, with a caveat that allows for maximum sentences to be subject to 5 year increments in the event of a prisoner not being rehabilitated).
